docs.title: About Me
docs.text:
I've spent 30+ years in the geospatial industry, most recently as a Division Chief at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, leading a 130+ person division and standing up enterprise GIS and foundation data programs. My career started hands-on, and since retiring in 2025 I've deliberately returned to that side of the work.

Lately that has meant earning seven AWS certifications, completing GIS programming and software design coursework at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and building geocrime-stl, an open-source Python ETL package, along with the St. Louis Crime Data Explorer built on top of it.

I'm looking for part-time, remote work as a geospatial analyst or data engineer, ideally with one team that can bring me in where the work is: a project, a data backlog, or coverage for a teammate who's out. I'm also open to contract engagements and the occasional strategy or advisory session.

docs.title: St. Louis Crime Data Explorer
docs.text: Crime map view: reported offenses within a half mile of a downtown address, with a breakdown by type, the most common offenses, and a month-by-month trend.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The St. Louis Crime Data Explorer is an interactive web dashboard that maps reported offenses in St. Louis at several spatial scales, from wards and neighborhoods down to a search radius around any address, so people can see the data at the point of need. It is built on monthly data prepared by the geocrime-stl ETL package.

Study Area: City of St. Louis, Missouri Role: Solo project (design, development, and documentation) Status: Live

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Data Source

  • SLMPD crime data as posted by the City of St. Louis, typically published around the 5th of the following month.
  • Coverage as of October 2026: 124,064 reported offenses from January 2024 through September 2026.
  • Offenses are grouped using the NIBRS "crimes against" classification: Person, Property, Society, plus Firearm and Other categories.

Features

  1. Map views: wards, neighborhoods, individual locations, and a heat layer.
  2. Address tools: address search, drop-a-pin, and use-my-location, with a "see crime near this address" option.
  3. Search radius: quarter-mile, half-mile, or one-mile.
  4. Filters: ward, neighborhood, offense category, and date.
  5. Analysis pages: Hotspots, Charts, and a Methodology page explaining how the data is prepared.
  6. Export: download the current list as CSV.

Tools Used

Tool Purpose geocrime-stl Monthly ETL: fetch, clean, standardize, clip to city boundaries City of St. Louis, OpenStreetMap, and U.S. Census geocoders Address search GitHub Pages Hosting Agentic, AI-assisted workflows Used to build and document the dashboard

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Multi-scale view: the same data can be read at the ward, neighborhood, or address-radius level.
  • Honest about limits: the site states plainly that these are reported offenses, not a measure of how safe a place is, and notes the limits of the data: block-level locations, per-victim counting, and reporting bias.
  • Privacy-minded: pins and device location stay in the browser; typed addresses go only to the geocoding services and are not stored.

The page layout was adapted from a crash-map project by Reddit user u/autosoap, used with permission.

docs.title: geocrime-stl: Open-Source ETL for St. Louis Crime Data
Overview
docs.text:
geocrime-stl is an open-source Python package that fetches, cleans, and standardizes monthly St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department (SLMPD) crime data so it is ready for spatial analysis. It is published on PyPI under the MIT License and is the data engine behind the St. Louis Crime Data Explorer.

Study Area: City of St. Louis, Missouri Role: Solo project (design, development, documentation, and publishing) Status: Released, version 0.2.0 (October 2026)

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Data Source

  • Publicly available monthly crime files from the SLMPD Stats page. The package depends on that site's availability and URL structure.

Processing Steps

  1. Fetch the monthly SLMPD file for the requested month and year.
  2. Clean and standardize the records into a consistent schema.
  3. Filter by time to keep only records from the target month, because SLMPD sometimes revises older records.
  4. Filter by space to drop records whose latitude and longitude fall outside the City of St. Louis boundaries.
  5. Export analysis-ready data as GeoJSON, GeoPackage, or CSV, with built-in monthly summaries and maps.

The pipeline at a glance: one monthly file in, analysis-ready files out.

A typical run is three calls: run_pipeline(4, 2026), then generate_monthly_metrics() for a monthly summary, then plot_monthly_maps() for the map quad shown below.

Example output

plot_monthly_maps() draws a four-panel matplotlib figure showing where reported incidents fall, for all incidents and for crimes against persons, property, and society. This is September 2026 (3,247 incidents).

Tools Used

Tool Purpose Python 3.11+ Package and pipeline code GeoJSON, GeoPackage, CSV Export formats for GIS and analysis tools PyPI Distribution (pip install geocrime-stl) MkDocs Material Documentation site with methodology page and API reference Jupyter notebooks Demo workflows for the ETL and hotspot analysis Agentic, AI-assisted workflows Used to build and document the package

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Turns a manual monthly download-and-cleanup chore into a repeatable, scripted pipeline.
  • Handles two data-quality issues that matter for mapping: revised historical records and coordinates that fall outside the city.
  • Documented for other users: installation and usage guides, FAQ, changelog, API reference for the extract, transform, monthly summary, and export modules, and demo notebooks.
